text:
Hi Steve, I love your videos, keep them coming! However, I need to point out a flaw in your price/performance comparison. Averaging frame rates between different games can lead to misleading or inaccurate results, because more emphasis is put on games with higher frame rates (which, ironically, are less demanding, and not reflective of current/future performance). Let me put it this way: let's say we have game 1 and game 2, GPU A and GPU B. Let's say both GPUs score 1000 FPS in game 1, and GPU A scores 10 FPS in game 2, while GPU B scores only 5 FPS in game 2. Therefore, on average, GPU A is 25% faster than GPU B, but they will have almost exactly the same price per frame, if both cost the same! But the logical conclusion is that GPU A is way better than B.
So, a way to deal with this is what you already do with percentages. You should pick a baseline (the 1080ti, for instance) and set that to 100%. Then compare the average percentage rate (as you already do) and divide these percentages with the price. This will give you a much, much better and accurate picture of price/performance.
author: @luisjalabert8366

text: Isn't this why you use a dozen samples?
author: @Hardwareunboxed

text:
@Hardwareunboxed  if the 'probability' distributions were the same, I'd agree, but it's not the case. It's true that using more samples can lead to better accuracy, but not necessarily true. Let's say you have 100 games, 50 of which GPU A and B both score 1000 FPS,  and in the other 50, GPU A scores 10 FPS, while GPU B scores 5 FPS. It would still be the case, that with 100 games, GPU A is 25% faster than B, but would have identical price per frame scores. You are just one step away from doing this the perfect way in any case!
You already did the percentage comparisons between the different GPUs (though you did it relative between a bunch of them instead of picking a baseline, but it should be almost the same calculation), so, the right way to do this would be say, pick the 2060 as a baseline (100). The 2060 super would be 109 (according to your 9% faster on average),  and the 2070 around 114 (I can't say exactly because I couldn't see a direct comparison between the 2060 and 2070). So what I would do is divide this number by the price, e.g., 100/330 = 0.303 for the 2060; 109/400 = 0.2725 for the 2060 super, and so on (higher is better in this case; if you want you can do price/percentage for lower is better).  In this case, since the differences in frame rates between different games isn't that big, the values are pretty similar with what you calculated, but if you include games such as GS GO, together with Assassin's creed or much more demanding games, your results could end up pretty skewed.

@zeroyum1473  theres some truth in that but ryzen 1 vs ryzen 2 was down to arch differences as much as anything.  as far the 12nm proces its just 16nm and they widened the gate a bit to get higher clocks which also lead to more power leakage. 



ryzen first gen has slower clocks but the tweak to the gates fixed that.  but even at the same clocks ryzen+ is faster because they tweaked the cache and the ccx latency.  that is an architectural difference and has nothing to do with processes maturing.


fabs have always said that processes take time to mature and blah blah blah but it was really about paying off the cost of the new equipment.  they had to charge more for the first couple years and bin chips lower so more would make the cut.  but it wasnt usually about the process maturing.  it was about the finances. in reality they usually had the next process after the "new" process ready to go and were just waiting to get their money out of the current process, basically staying one process behind what they were really capapble of.


but now that BS talk they used to use to get more money out of a new process is actually true.  no more having the next process in teh bag before the "new" one even rolls out.  its actually true now.


they have 2 choices, double the pattern count and go from dual to quad patterning when dual patterning in the first place gave them fits.  so once again they have to double the chances of a defect and get worse yields.  about 70% on an 8 core die with have the stuff thats normally on a cpu die being moved out to about 90+% on 14nm (either intel or anybody else that makes 14nm). 



the other choice is EUV which has its own problems (which will be fixed).  but once you fix those problems you have the problem of power draw. not in the chip but at the plant that makes them.  it takes, i think, 1 million watts of electricity to get the 200w of EUV light energy used by just one litho machine.  thats an insane inefficiency and it takes weeks to just finish one wafer.  that light is not on that wafer all the time but still its a huge energy cost.


both intel and amd have both chosen to go with quad patterning till the problems with EUV are fixed.  intel chose to only do it on the mobile products and even then only on the high end ones.


amd have chosen to only use quad patterning on the cores themselves and eveyrthing else on 14nm.


these are sings that the old "problems" that fabs used to get higher prices are actually real now.  and they are probalby chargin more than ever and getting worse yields on top of that

sure the yields for the process improved....1-2 years ago.  after that its probably been super high the whole time.  by the time you factor in the fact that they have extra cuda cores to cut off,  the 2060 die probalby had 90% yields (that is to say that a tu 106 die had a 90% chance of being a full 2070 or a 2060 at least).  the 2080 a bit less, maybe 70% but all those dies that didnt make it were saved for the 2070 super which would probalby boost it to around 90%.
